results.summary: This project is an interactive Morse Code trainer that displays letters on a 7-segment display and challenges the user to input the correct Morse pattern using a switch. It provides immediate feedback and progresses through the English alphabet. The design can be tested in simulation or on hardware, though the documentation does not specify external hardware requirements beyond the 7-segment display and input switch. The project is notable for being a simple educational game implemented in Verilog.

This project is a gate test that allows the user to experiment with different logic gates by toggling switches and observing outputs. It is implemented in Wokwi and requires switches and a single-number LED display as external hardware. The documentation is minimal, describing only that inputs and outputs are interconnected between gates. It serves as a basic educational tool for understanding logic gate behavior.

This design displays a bouncing ROOTS logo with an animated color gradient and a kaleidoscope background on a VGA monitor. It is implemented in Verilog and requires a Tiny VGA Pmod for external hardware. The design is tested by connecting to a VGA monitor and configuring inputs. It is notable for being a simple graphics demo with a specific visual theme.

This project implements a variable-length LFSR with 2-tap and 4-tap configurations, featuring hold and step controls. It uses a length-to-mask table selected by n_taps, and outputs a 15-bit value with a valid signal. The design was tested using hand-generated test modules and GTK signal evaluation, but no formal test is included. It requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout board, and is notable for its flexible configuration and hold/step functionality.

Borg is a tiny GPU built around a RISC-V SoC (TinyQV) that renders a 10-frame animation of a rotating RGB triangle entirely from firmware. It is implemented in Chisel and requires a QSPI Pmod for external memory, with FPGA development using a pico-ice board and Raspberry Pi Debug Probe. Testing involves programming the firmware and reading back PPM images. The design is notable for integrating a GPU with a RISC-V core on a small scale.

This chip implements a character-level language model with ternary weights baked into ROM, generating Shakespeare-style text one character at a time. It uses a host microcontroller (RP2350B) to handle character tables and sampling, communicating via a byte protocol. The design is tested with reference firmware on the Tiny Tapeout demo board, requiring no external hardware beyond the board. It is notable for its compact ROM-based model and efficient 5-lane arithmetic unit.

This project implements a simplified 6502-inspired 8-bit microprocessor with a central ALU, registers, and a microcoded instruction decoder executing a subset of the 6502 instruction set. It is written in Verilog and includes a block diagram. Testing strategies are described but not detailed in the provided documentation. The design is notable for being a custom, reduced version of the classic 6502 architecture.

This project is a Morse code generator for the letters J and R, using a 4-bit synchronous counter and logic gates to produce dot and dash patterns. It is implemented in Wokwi and requires a button, 7-segment display, and clock as external hardware. Testing involves connecting the display and changing inputs with a button. The design is notable for its simplicity and educational value in demonstrating Morse code encoding.

DUMBRV is a simple RISC-V processor supporting the RV32E base instruction set plus Zicond and Zbs extensions, using two independent SPI memories for instructions and data. It requires one 512Kbit ROM and one 512Kbit RAM, and is tested with a program that records and outputs GPIO sequences. The design is notable for its dual SPI memory architecture and minimalistic RISC-V implementation.

This project attempts to create a random number generator using the unstable state of a latch when both S and R inputs are set to 0. It includes 34 instances per output pin to increase chances of randomness, with a freeze input to sample values. The documentation is uncertain about its functionality, noting potential bias or constant output. It is notable for its experimental and humorous approach, with pin names like 'trump_tarifs' and 'lottery_winning_number'.
